title: The Catch-All of Life
question: What counts as a protist?
hook: Biology has a group that is defined only by what it is not.
idea: Protists are all eukaryotes that are not animals, land plants or fungi, so no single trait unites them.

beats.prompt: Biologists look for one feature that every protist has and no other organism has. What do they find?

choices.label: All protists are single-celled
choices.feedback: Tempting, but several transitions to multicellularity have occurred among protists, such as seaweeds with differentiated tissues.

choices.label: All protists have chloroplasts
choices.feedback: Many do not: the remaining heterotrophic protists are often called protozoa.

choices.label: None; the group is defined by exclusion

beats.explain: Protists are defined as all eukaryotes that are not animals, land plants or fungi, so there is no unique trait that unifies all protists yet excludes non-protists.

beats.prompt: Sort each group by whether it counts as protist.
beats.explain: The protist label excludes animals, land plants and all fungi, but includes all eukaryotic algae and fungus-like groups such as the oomycetes.

beats.prompt: Match each supergroup to what it contains.
pairs: Mostly red and green algae, from which land plants evolved
Fungi, animals and their single-celled relatives
The earliest diverging groups of flagellates
beats.explain: Modern classifications spread protists across several large clades known as supergroups.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Protists are defined as all eukaryotes that are not animals, land plants or fungi.
The ancestors of those three groups evolved from protists.
So protists do not form a natural group, or clade.
So one trait must unite all protists while excluding all non-protists.
beats.explain: Because protists are defined by exclusion, there is no unique trait that unifies all protists yet excludes non-protists.
